docs.text: Q Answer Explanation 1 A PSIAs are Mudarabah contracts — the bank manages funds as Mudarib, depositors provide capital as Rab al-Mal and bear investment losses. There is no capital guarantee. 2 B Commodity Murabaha is the primary Islamic interbank placement mechanism — banks buy and sell commodities (e.g., base metals via LME or Bursa Suq Al-Sila') to generate Shariah-compliant fund transfers. 3 D DCR is the pressure on Islamic banks to pay PSIA holders competitive (conventional) returns even when actual investment performance is lower — requiring the bank to absorb the shortfall from its own equity. 4 C The OIC Fiqh Academy's 2009 resolution found that organised Tawarruq without genuine commodity movement replicates interest-bearing lending in substance — the core scholarly objection. 5 B IILM issues short-term investment-grade sukuk designed to qualify as Basel III HQLAs, solving the liquidity management gap for Islamic banks that cannot hold conventional government bonds.

docs.title: Module 6: Sukuk and Public Capital Markets
6.1 Sukuk Definition and Economic Role
docs.text:
Sukuk, often referred to as "Shariah-compliant bonds," are formally defined as Islamic financial certificates that represent an undivided ownership share in an underlying tangible asset, project, or specialized investing activity. The global standard for these instruments is established by the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) under Shari'ah Standard No. 17 (Investment Sukuk). AAOIFI SS 17 strictly defines sukuk as "certificates of equal value representing undivided shares in ownership of tangible assets, usufruct and services or (in the ownership of) the assets of particular projects or special investment activity".

The Distinction from Conventional Bonds While sukuk serve a similar economic function to conventional bonds in raising capital, their legal and structural foundations are fundamentally different. A conventional bond is a pure debt obligation (an IOU) in which the issuer borrows money and promises to repay the principal with interest.

Because Islamic law explicitly forbids the charging or paying of interest (riba), sukuk must be backed by real, Shariah-compliant assets or business ventures. Instead of receiving fixed interest payments, sukuk investors earn returns generated by the actual performance of the underlying asset—such as rental income, profit-sharing, or a combination thereof. Consequently, sukuk holders inherently share in the commercial risks and rewards associated with the asset's ownership, aligning with the Islamic principle of risk-sharing.

Market Scale and Growth The global sukuk market has achieved massive scale, transitioning from a niche ethical product to a mainstream fixture in global capital markets. According to the International Islamic Financial Market (IIFM), total global sukuk issuances reached US$ 205 billion in 2024.

Within this total, international sukuk issuances hit a record high of US$ 65.6 billion in 2024, representing a 24.5% increase from the previous year, driven by favorable global liquidity conditions and declining funding costs. As a result of this continued momentum, total outstanding sukuk surpassed the US$ 900 billion mark, with several broader industry reports projecting or confirming the market successfully crossing the US$ 1 trillion threshold globally in 2024.

Sovereign Sukuk as the Market Anchor Sovereign sukuk act as the critical anchor segment for the broader Islamic capital markets. For governments, issuing sovereign sukuk is a strategic tool to diversify their investor base, allowing them to tap into vast pools of Islamic liquidity and ethical investors who avoid conventional interest-bearing debt.

More importantly, sovereign issuances lay the groundwork for a healthy financial ecosystem. They establish vital pricing benchmarks and local-currency yield curves that facilitate and encourage private sector and corporate issuances. Additionally, sovereign sukuk provide essential high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) that central banks and Islamic financial institutions use for robust liquidity management and monetary policy operations.

docs.title: 6.2 Asset-Based vs Asset-Backed: The Critical Distinction
docs.text:
The most important structural distinction in the Islamic capital markets revolves around how a sukuk (Islamic investment certificate) allocates risk and ownership between the issuer and the investors. While both structures aim to comply with Islamic prohibitions on interest (riba) and excessive uncertainty (gharar), they function very differently in practice.

Asset-Based Sukuk (Dominant, Credit Reliance) The vast majority of sukuk issued today—up to 90% or 95% of the market—are structured as asset-based securities. In an asset-based structure, the originator identifies a pool of Shariah-compliant assets to facilitate the transaction, but no "true sale" or legal transfer of ownership takes place. Instead, investors are only granted a "beneficial ownership" interest in the assets.

Because legal title remains with the originator on their balance sheet, investors do not bear the genuine risks of owning the asset. More importantly, investors have no direct recourse to the underlying assets in the event of a default. Instead, the investors rely entirely on the creditworthiness of the originator (the obligor). To mimic the fixed-income characteristics and capital preservation of a conventional bond, these structures utilize a "purchase undertaking" (a binding promise) where the originator agrees to buy back the assets at maturity or upon default for a predetermined fixed price—usually the exact face value of the original investment. In substance, this replicates a conventional unsecured corporate loan.

Asset-Backed Sukuk (True Sale, Genuine Risk Transfer) Conversely, an asset-backed sukuk involves a "true sale" where the legal title and ownership of the underlying assets are genuinely transferred from the originator to a bankruptcy-remote Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV).

In this structure, the core Islamic principle of al-ghunm wa al-ghurm (entitlement to gain is justified only by bearing risk) is fully realized. Sukuk holders assume the genuine risks and rewards associated with the asset's performance. There is no guarantee of principal return; if the underlying asset underperforms, is damaged, or drops in market value, the investors bear the financial loss. Because the assets are completely separated from the originator's books, investors have direct recourse to the assets themselves, shielding them from the originator's potential bankruptcy. While highly favored by Shariah purists for their authenticity, asset-backed sukuk are relatively rare due to legal complexities and lower investor appetite for actual equity-like risk.

The 2008 AAOIFI Sukuk Statement The tension between these two structures reached a boiling point in late 2007 when Sheikh Muhammad Taqi Usmani, Chairman of the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) Shariah board, publicly estimated that 85% of outstanding sukuk failed to comply with core Shariah principles. He criticized asset-based structures—particularly those using mudaraba and musharaka (partnership) contracts—for utilizing purchase undertakings that guaranteed the return of principal, arguing they were effectively conventional debt instruments.

In response, AAOIFI issued a landmark pronouncement in February 2008 outlining strict rules to realign the market. The 2008 Statement mandated that:

  • Sukuk must represent genuine ownership with all its rights and obligations.

  • Managers or agents cannot offer loans to investors to cover earnings shortfalls.

  • Most crucially, originators cannot undertake to repurchase equity-based assets at their nominal (face) value at maturity or default. Any repurchase must be executed at the asset's net, market, or fair value at the time of the sale, forcing investors to bear actual market risk.

The 2008 Statement caused a sharp decline in musharaka and mudaraba sukuk issuances, leading the market to heavily favor ijara (lease-based) structures where it was easier to compliantly structure predictable, bond-like returns.

The AAOIFI Standard 62 Debate The debate between legal form and economic substance is currently being tested again with AAOIFI's proposed Shariah Standard No. 62, drafted in late 2023. Standard 62 seeks to completely overhaul the market by mandating the actual legal transfer of ownership (true sale) of underlying assets from issuers to investors, eliminating implicit and explicit capital guarantees, and effectively forcing the market into true asset-backed structures.

This has sparked a massive debate regarding Shariah Authenticity vs. Market Stability:

  • Shariah Authenticity: Standard 62 successfully realigns sukuk with their intended religious purpose as risk-sharing investment certificates. It answers long-standing criticisms that Islamic finance is merely conventional finance repackaged with Arabic terminology.

  • Market Stability & Disruption: Industry participants heavily warn that a strict implementation of Standard 62 could destabilize the $1.2 trillion sukuk market. True asset sales incur massive transaction costs, trigger heavy tax implications, and are legally difficult in jurisdictions that restrict foreign ownership of sovereign assets.

  • Credit Ratings and Fragmentation: If sukuk transition to variable-return, genuine risk-sharing instruments, traditional credit rating agencies may view them as equity rather than debt, rendering them "unrateable" under standard fixed-income methodologies. Furthermore, analysts fear severe market fragmentation; GCC countries may strictly adopt Standard 62, while major hubs like Malaysia—which relies on its own flexible Shariah framework—may ignore it, fracturing global Islamic liquidity.

Consequently, policymakers and regulators are currently exploring "phased adoption" frameworks to balance the religious mandate for asset-backed authenticity against the commercial need for market continuity and stable pricing.

docs.title: 6.3 Sukuk Structure Menu
docs.text:
Ijara Sukuk (Lease-Based) The Ijara Sukuk functions as a lease-based financial mechanism where an originator sells a tangible asset to a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV), which subsequently leases it back to the originator. The periodic rental payments form the returns passed on to the Sukuk holders. Because this structure represents undivided beneficial ownership in the usufruct of physical assets rather than just financial debt, it is highly tradable in secondary markets. For this reason, along with its easily understood lease economics, Ijara is the most widely used structure for sovereign issuances, prominently utilized by governments such as the UK, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE.

Wakala Sukuk (Agency-Based) Wakala Sukuk operate on an investment agency contract where investors appoint an agent (wakeel) to manage funds with the goal of generating an expected profit return. This structure provides high flexibility for diversifying pools of assets, allowing originators (such as Islamic banks) to bundle various Shariah-compliant investments—including lease contracts, equities, and Murabaha receivables—when a single large tangible asset is unavailable. Because the agent exercises significant control over the portfolio, this structure requires robust and unambiguous agency agreements that clearly define the investment criteria, duration, fee structure, and termination conditions. In this arrangement, the investors receive the pre-agreed profit return, while the wakeel typically retains any excess profit as a performance incentive fee.

Murabaha & Salam Sukuk (Sale-Based & Debt) Murabaha Sukuk are based on cost-plus-profit sales, where the issuer acquires commodities and sells them at a disclosed markup on deferred payment terms. Salam Sukuk involve a forward sale where payment is made upfront for future delivery of goods. Both structures face severe tradability constraints because their issuance predominantly generates debt receivables rather than tangible ownership. Under Islamic jurisprudence, trading in debt at a discount or premium is considered riba (interest). AAOIFI Shariah Standard No. 59 on the Sale of Debt (Bay' al-Dayn) explicitly restricts the secondary market trading of such monetary debts, stipulating they cannot be traded except strictly at par value. Therefore, these Sukuk can generally only become negotiable if they constitute a highly restricted, small fraction of a larger portfolio that is predominantly backed by tangible assets.

Musharaka & Mudaraba Sukuk (Equity-Based Partnerships) These are equity-based partnership structures built on the core Islamic principle of profit and loss sharing (PLS). Musharaka is a joint venture where all parties contribute capital and share profits and losses, while Mudaraba is a trustee partnership involving a capital provider (Rab-al-Maal) and an entrepreneur/manager (Mudarib). In 2008, the AAOIFI issued a critical statement asserting that up to 85% of existing Sukuk failed Shariah substance requirements because they utilized fixed-price purchase undertakings. These undertakings virtually guaranteed the return of principal by forcing the originator to buy back the partnership assets at face value, making them economically identical to conventional guaranteed debt. To ensure genuine profit and loss sharing, the 2008 AAOIFI requirements dictate that any repurchase of the underlying partnership assets must occur at net asset value or fair market value at the time of sale, forcing investors to bear true equity risk.

Hybrid Sukuk To balance stringent Shariah structural requirements with practical market demands for liquidity, issuers frequently utilize Hybrid Sukuk, which combine multiple Islamic contracts (e.g., combining Istisna with Ijara, or Wakala with Murabaha). This approach allows originators to tap into capital markets even if their balance sheets are heavy with non-tradable debt receivables. However, to ensure these hybrid instruments remain tradable in the secondary market, Shariah scholars mandate a minimum tangible asset ratio—commonly ranging from 33% to 51% of the total underlying portfolio—to ensure the Sukuk represents a genuine ownership interest rather than pure debt.

docs.title: 6.4 Secondary Market Issues
docs.text:
AAOIFI Shariah Standard 59 and the Sale of Debt (Bay' al-Dayn) In Islamic finance, the secondary market is heavily governed by the prohibition of riba (interest) and the requirement that transactions be linked to real economic activity. AAOIFI Shariah Standard No. 59 on the Sale of Debt establishes strict boundaries for trading financial obligations. The standard explicitly prohibits selling a monetary debt for cash or another monetary debt, as exchanging money for money at a discount or premium constitutes riba. While a monetary debt can be sold for a commodity, usufruct, or service with spot delivery, it cannot be sold for a commodity with deferred delivery, nor can it be sold to a third party if it involves excessive gharar (uncertainty).

Tradability Requirements for Tangible Assets and Usufruct Interests Because trading pure debt is prohibited, for an Islamic financial instrument (like a Sukuk) to be freely negotiable in the secondary market, it must represent an undivided ownership interest in tangible assets, usufructs (the right to use an asset), or services.

If a portfolio is mixed—containing cash, debt receivables, and physical assets—it can only be traded if it meets specific tangibility ratios. SS 59 mandates that tangible assets and usufructs must form a substantial portion of the portfolio. While historically some scholars accepted a minimum of 30% tangible assets, others required 51% to 70%. Under SS 59, the ratio of tangible assets must generally exceed 50% for an entity's assets to be freely securitized and traded. However, the standard stipulates an absolute floor: the ratio of tangible assets must never fall below 33% of the total asset value at any time.

How This Shapes Portfolio Composition The strict tradability requirements of SS 59 profoundly shape how issuers construct and manage their asset portfolios:

  • Hybrid Structuring: To achieve desired cash-flow targets while remaining tradable, issuers frequently design "hybrid sukuk." These portfolios combine non-tradable debt contracts (like Murabaha or Istisna'a) with tradable, asset-backed contracts (like Ijara or equities) to ensure the tangible portion meets the 30–51% threshold.

  • Active Maintenance of Tangibility: SS 59 introduced a dynamic requirement meaning the tangibility ratio is not just an issuance threshold, but an ongoing maintenance requirement. If the tangible asset value drops below 33% during the life of the instrument, the Sukuk becomes non-negotiable (except under the strict rules of debt trading at par value). If listed on an exchange, a Sukuk breaching this threshold must be delisted, forcing issuers to actively manage asset compositions and substitute assets to maintain liquidity.

  • Use of Usufructs (Manafa'a): When physical assets are unavailable or encumbered, portfolio managers can utilize intangible usufruct rights (such as airtime vouchers, toll road concessions, or electricity tariffs) to satisfy the tangible asset requirement, allowing the portfolio to be traded.

Limitations on Certain Structures The prohibition on the sale of debt and the tangibility requirements severely limit the liquidity and secondary market viability of several Islamic financial structures:

  • Murabaha Sukuk: Murabaha is a cost-plus deferred payment sale, meaning it inherently creates a monetary debt receivable. Because they represent debt rather than physical assets, Murabaha Sukuk cannot be traded on the secondary market at a premium or discount. They must be held to maturity or traded only at par value, making them highly illiquid. (An exception exists in Malaysia, where local jurists have historically permitted the trading of debt (bay' al-dayn), allowing secondary trading of Murabaha Sukuk, though this is rejected by GCC scholars).

  • Salam and Istisna'a Sukuk: Salam contracts involve advance payment for the future delivery of goods. Because they represent a debt liability for future delivery, Salam certificates are strictly non-tradable. Similarly, Istisna'a (manufacturing) certificates can only be traded once the funds have been converted into owned physical assets; if the asset has already been delivered to the ultimate buyer, the certificate represents a monetary debt and loses its tradability.

  • Distressed Debt and Private Credit: The rules under SS 59 deeply constrain distressed debt strategies. In conventional finance, distressed receivables are frequently bought and sold at a discount. In Islamic private markets, the discounted purchase of receivables is forbidden, forcing restructuring strategies to rely on complex asset sales, novation, or equity-based restructurings rather than simple debt trading.

docs.title: 6.5 Equity Screening and Listed Products
docs.text:
The global Islamic equity market is a massive and rapidly maturing segment of the financial system, acting as the gatekeeper for an estimated USD 4.3 trillion screened universe. To ensure that investments align with Islamic law, stock selection relies on a rigorous two-stage architecture: business activity screening (qualitative) and financial ratio screening (quantitative).

Business Activity Screens The primary step in Shariah screening involves excluding companies whose core business operations fall into prohibited (haram) sectors. Common exclusions across all major indices include conventional interest-based financial services (such as banking and insurance), alcohol, pork-related products, gambling and casinos, adult entertainment, weapons and defense, and tobacco.

Because complete purity is rare in modern multinational conglomerates, most Shariah boards and index providers tolerate a de minimis level of non-permissible activity. The standard rule is that revenue from non-permissible sources must not exceed 5% of a company’s total income. Even when a company passes this screen, Muslim investors are obligated to undergo a purification process—calculating the exact percentage of the company's dividend or profit derived from these haram sources and donating that equivalent amount to charity.

Financial Ratio Screens Since it is virtually impossible to find public companies completely free of conventional bank accounts or interest-bearing debt, Shariah scholars established quantitative tolerance thresholds. These screens are designed to limit a portfolio's indirect exposure to riba (interest) and typically evaluate three core areas:

  1. Leverage (Debt Ratio): Interest-bearing debt compared to a specific denominator.

  2. Liquidity (Cash Ratio): Cash and interest-bearing securities compared to a denominator.

  3. Receivables Ratio: Accounts receivable compared to a denominator.

Global index providers apply these principles differently, specifically regarding whether they use Total Assets or Market Capitalization as the denominator for these ratios, which can lead to the same company passing one index's screen while failing another's.

MSCI Islamic Index The standard MSCI Islamic Index series employs a balance-sheet approach, using Total Assets (TA) as its primary denominator.

  • Thresholds: It restricts total debt, cash and interest-bearing securities, and the sum of accounts receivable plus cash to each be strictly less than 33.33% of total assets.

  • MSCI also applies a stricter business activity screen by specifically excluding companies involved in hotels, cinemas, and music from its investment universe.

  • To accommodate different investor preferences, MSCI also offers an "M-Series" variant, which calculates ratios against Average Market Capitalization instead of Total Assets.

Dow Jones Islamic Market (DJIM) Historically, DJIM structured its financial screens against a 24-month trailing average market capitalization to smooth out the volatility of daily stock prices.

  • Thresholds: Its traditional rulebook capped total debt, cash plus interest-bearing securities, and accounts receivable at a strict 33% each.

  • Recent Changes: In a highly notable methodology update in September 2023, DJIM eliminated its cash and accounts receivable screens entirely. It now evaluates compliance based solely on the 33% debt-to-market-cap limit and the 5% impure income threshold, significantly expanding its pool of eligible equities.

S&P Shariah S&P applies a methodology similar to DJIM but traditionally utilizes a 36-month average market capitalization to calculate its ratios.

  • Thresholds: It capped debt and cash at 33%, but was uniquely lenient on accounts receivable, allowing them to comprise up to 49% of the 36-month average market capitalization.

  • Recent Changes: Mirroring DJIM, S&P also removed its cash and receivables screening requirements in September 2023, moving to a simplified leverage-and-revenue-only screening model.

docs.title: 6.6 Islamic REITs and ETFs
docs.text:
Islamic Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs)

Islamic REITs function similarly to conventional REITs by offering investors pooled access to real estate, but they are strictly governed by Shariah principles regarding their investments, tenants, and capital structures. Malaysia is the principal jurisdiction and global leader in establishing regulatory frameworks for Islamic REITs. The Securities Commission Malaysia (SC) has issued comprehensive Guidelines for Islamic REITs that provide Shariah guidance on business activities, complementing the existing conventional REIT frameworks.

Shariah-Compliant Tenants and Mixed Activities A fundamental requirement for an Islamic REIT is that its tenants must operate permissible businesses. The REIT cannot lease space for haram (prohibited) activities, such as conventional interest-based banking, non-Takaful insurance, gambling, pornography, or the manufacture and sale of alcohol, tobacco, arms, and pork products.

However, to accommodate commercial realities, the SC's Shariah Advisory Council (SAC) allows Islamic REITs to acquire properties with tenants engaged in "mixed activities," provided the rental income from non-permissible activities does not exceed a 20% benchmark of the REIT's total turnover.

  • If the non-permissible rental income exceeds 20%, the Shariah adviser must instruct the fund manager not to invest in that property.

  • An Islamic REIT is strictly prohibited from acquiring a property where all tenants operate non-permissible activities (e.g., a casino building), even if the total rental income falls below the 20% threshold.

  • For vacant properties seeking new tenants, the REIT cannot accept operators of fully non-permissible activities.

  • To calculate the non-permissible rental portion for a tenant operating mixed activities (e.g., a supermarket selling both halal groceries and alcohol), the REIT can use the ratio of the physical floor area dedicated to the non-permissible activity against the total rented area.

Financing, Insurance, and Operations Islamic REITs must exclusively use Shariah-compliant instruments for all investments, deposits, and financing. Conventional debt leverage is prohibited and must be replaced by Islamic financing facilities. Furthermore, Islamic REITs must insure their real estate assets using Takaful (Islamic insurance) schemes, though conventional insurance is temporarily permitted if appropriate Takaful coverage is unavailable. For risk management, they are permitted to participate in forward foreign exchange sales or purchases, ideally utilizing the Islamic concept of wa'd (promise) with Islamic financial institutions. A practical example of a Malaysian Islamic REIT is the Al-Salam REIT, which holds Shariah-compliant assets such as QSR Brands (KFC and Pizza Hut) properties, retail malls, and office buildings.

Islamic Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) and the iShares Sukuk UCITS ETF

Islamic ETFs are passively managed open-ended funds that track Shariah-compliant indices, providing investors with a cost-effective, transparent, and diversified way to access halal equities and fixed-income alternatives.

A prominent example in the fixed-income space is the iShares $ Sukuk UCITS ETF (ticker: SKUK), managed by BlackRock.

  • Investment Objective: The fund aims to reflect the total return performance of the J.P. Morgan EM Aggregate Sukuk Index.

  • Asset Composition: It measures the performance of US Dollar-denominated emerging market Sukuk issued by sovereign, quasi-sovereign, corporate, and supranational entities.

  • Shariah Compliance: The tracked index strictly includes instruments labeled as Sukuk that comply with the standards set by the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI).

  • Structure: It is a physical, sampled ETF domiciled in Ireland, with its base currency in USD.

Challenges in the Islamic ETF Market While Islamic ETFs like the iShares Sukuk UCITS ETF offer vital market access, they face unique structural hurdles. Passive Sukuk funds and ETFs often carry higher management fees than their conventional counterparts. This is driven by the additional costs of annual Shariah board audits, continuous compliance screening, and the requirement to identify and "purify" (donate to charity) any incidental non-compliant income. Additionally, because many Sukuk investors adopt a "buy-and-hold" strategy, secondary market liquidity is often low. This can increase trading costs and make it challenging for ETF managers to perfectly replicate index benchmarks without experiencing price volatility.

docs.title: 6.7 ESG and Sustainable Sukuk
docs.text:
The convergence of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) criteria with Islamic finance is driven by a profound natural synergy between sustainable investing and Maqasid al-Shariah (the objectives of Islamic law). Islamic finance inherently promotes ethical conduct, social justice, and environmental stewardship, viewing humans as trustees (khalifah) of the Earth. It relies on risk-sharing, asset-backed transactions, and positive societal impact (maslahah), while strictly prohibiting riba (interest), gharar (excessive uncertainty), maysir (speculation), and investments in harmful sectors. This dual emphasis on avoiding harm through negative screening and promoting sustainable economic activity aligns seamlessly with global ESG mandates.

Driven by this alignment and the urgent need for climate finance, the sustainable sukuk market has experienced record growth. In 2024, global issuances of ESG sukuk reached US$ 15.4 billion, representing a 14.7% increase from the previous year and pushing the total outstanding value of ESG sukuk past the US$ 50 billion milestone. Green sukuk issuances alone exceeded USD 15 billion in 2024, heavily bolstered by commitments from GCC countries to fund energy transition targets, green infrastructure, and net-zero initiatives.

To standardize this rapid expansion and foster international trust, the International Capital Market Association (ICMA), the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB), and the London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) jointly published the "Guidance on Green, Social and Sustainability Sukuk" in April 2024. This landmark guidance bridges sustainable finance conventions with Islamic structuring, confirming the wide applicability of the ICMA Principles (such as the Green Bond Principles and Sustainability Bond Guidelines) to the global sukuk market. The framework helps issuers appropriately label their sukuk, navigate the complex dual-approval issuance process, and align with international ESG standards, ultimately making sustainable sukuk more accessible to conventional ESG investors who prioritize sustainability over strict Shariah compliance.

Malaysia has served as a pioneering force in this ecosystem, having introduced the Sustainable and Responsible Investment (SRI) Sukuk Framework through its Securities Commission (SC) in 2014. Under this framework, proceeds must be applied exclusively to eligible SRI projects, which encompass green initiatives (like renewable energy and energy efficiency), social projects (like affordable housing and healthcare), and waqf (endowment) asset development. Furthermore, the SC has established advanced requirements for SRI-linked sukuk, an innovative structure where the financial or structural characteristics of the sukuk (such as the profit rate) vary dynamically depending on whether the issuer meets predefined Sustainability Performance Targets (SPTs) measured against Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). Due to this highly supportive regulatory scaffolding, SRI sukuk issuances in Malaysia have surged nearly ninefold since their inception, reaching RM 11.9 billion in 2024.

Despite the tremendous growth and synergies, the convergence of these two financial systems introduces the dual risk of "greenwashing" and "Shariah-washing". Greenwashing occurs when the environmental or social benefits of the funded projects are overstated, lack credible KPIs, or fail to deliver the expected impact. Shariah-washing arises when sukuk mimic conventional debt in their economic substance—such as relying on binding purchase undertakings that guarantee the principal and eliminate true profit-and-loss sharing—despite bearing a superficial "Shariah-compliant" legal form. To mitigate these intersecting reputational risks, market participants must ensure rigorous compliance through transparent use-of-proceeds reporting, credible external reviews (Second Party Opinions), and robust, independent Shariah governance mechanisms that verify both the ethical impact and the jurisprudential validity of the instruments.

docs.title: Executive Refresher
docs.text:
• Sukuk Are Not Bonds with a Shariah Label: Sukuk represent proportionate beneficial ownership in an underlying asset, usufruct, or project — not a debt claim against the issuer. This fundamental distinction drives differences in documentation (trust structure, asset register, transfer restrictions), tax treatment (transfer taxes on asset sales), and insolvency treatment (asset-backed investors have a property claim, not a creditor claim). Practitioners who treat sukuk as conventional bonds with extra documentation consistently miss material risks.

  • AAOIFI SS 17 Changed the Market Landscape: The 2008 AAOIFI opinion clarified that purchase undertakings guaranteeing repayment of face value may violate Shariah by eliminating the investor's exposure to asset risk. While the market largely continues using purchase undertakings (particularly for IG corporate sukuk), the scholarly debate this triggered has driven the growth of more genuinely asset-backed structures — and is a live risk factor for sukuk outstanding in jurisdictions with activist Shariah authorities.

  • Asset-Based vs Asset-Backed is a Credit and Legal Distinction: In an asset-based sukuk, investors rely on the issuer's credit and a purchase undertaking — the asset reference is the source of Shariah compliance, not investor protection. In a true asset-backed sukuk, a perfected true-sale transfers legal ownership to the SPV and investors have enforceable security over the assets in default. This distinction must be clearly communicated to investors and documented in the prospectus — it is among the most important disclosures in Islamic capital markets.

  • Sukuk Default Mechanics Differ from Bond Default: Sukuk default triggers, enforcement rights, and resolution mechanisms are more complex than equivalent bond structures. Acceleration typically requires dissolution of the underlying asset arrangement — creating timing and valuation challenges. The Dana Gas case demonstrated that an issuer's challenge to the Shariah validity of its own instruments can create profound legal uncertainty. Always review the dissolution event provisions, governing law, and enforcement jurisdiction before investing.

  • Green and ESG Sukuk Represent the Growth Frontier: The alignment between Islamic finance's prohibition on harmful activities and ESG frameworks creates a natural overlap in green sukuk. Practitioners should note that 'green' and 'Shariah-compliant' are independently assessed — a sukuk can be one without being the other — and dual-certification requires separate documentation and verification for each framework.

docs.title: Module 7: Islamic Finance in Private Markets
7.1 Why Private Markets Are the Natural Home
docs.text:
Why Private Markets Suit Islamic Finance

Private markets—encompassing private equity (PE), venture capital (VC), private credit, and infrastructure—are widely considered the "truest" and most natural frontier for Islamic finance. Unlike conventional banking, which revolves around the time value of money and interest-based lending, Islamic finance is a constraint-driven system that demands a rigid linkage between financial capital and real economic activity.

The structural alignment between private markets and Islamic finance rests on three core pillars:

  • Risk-Sharing (Profit and Loss Sharing - PLS): Islamic jurisprudence forbids riba (interest) and instead legitimizes returns through the active assumption of commercial risk. The conventional General Partner/Limited Partner (GP/LP) structure perfectly mirrors the classical Islamic Mudarabah (trustee partnership) and Musharakah (joint venture) contracts. In a Mudarabah fund, the LPs act as the Rab-al-Maal (capital providers) who bear the financial risk, while the GP acts as the Mudarib (manager) who provides expertise. Profits are shared based on pre-agreed ratios (like carried interest), while financial losses are borne solely by the capital providers, perfectly aligning the risk-reward ethos of both PE and Shariah.

  • Direct Ownership: Islamic finance strictly prohibits gharar (excessive uncertainty) and maysir (speculation/gambling). While public market trading can sometimes border on short-term speculation, private market investments involve direct, long-term equity ownership and active management in target companies. This active involvement reduces information asymmetry and fulfills the Shariah requirement for transparent, participatory business relationships.

  • Real-Economy Linkage (Material Finality): A fundamental rule of Islamic finance is that every transaction must be linked to a tangible asset, usufruct, or legitimate service. Private equity and venture capital inherently inject capital directly into startups, real estate, and infrastructure to build businesses and generate jobs. This direct value creation fulfills the Islamic objective of promoting societal welfare (Maqasid al-Shariah) and avoids the "financialization" or decoupling of finance from the real economy seen in synthetic derivatives and conventional debt trading.

Friction from Conventional Norms

Despite this ideological harmony, severe structural friction arises when Islamic funds interact with standard Western private market mechanics. Conventional PE and VC heavily rely on downside protections and debt-driven returns that fundamentally clash with Shariah law.

1. Liquidation Preferences and Convertible Notes In conventional VC, investors frequently utilize preference shares and convertible notes to protect their downside. A liquidation preference guarantees that if a company is sold or liquidated, the preferred investors receive their capital back before common shareholders see any return.

  • The Shariah Clash: The Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) and the International Islamic Fiqh Academy strictly prohibit preference shares that guarantee capital preservation or prioritize one partner over another in liquidation. Shariah dictates that partners must share losses strictly in proportion to their capital contributions. Furthermore, standard convertible notes often function as interest-bearing debt that converts to equity, directly violating the ban on riba.

  • Islamic Alternatives: To replicate these protections credibly without "cosmetic replication," Islamic funds may use dual-class shares with variable profit-sharing ratios, or apply the concept of tanazul—where common shareholders willingly forego their right to equal standing in a liquidation scenario. For venture debt, equity kickers are structured using a Wa'd (unilateral binding promise to sell shares) rather than standard speculative warrants.

2. Preferred Returns (Hurdle Rates) Conventional private equity funds typically offer LPs a "preferred return" or "hurdle rate" (e.g., a guaranteed 8% annual return) before the GP can collect carried interest.

  • The Shariah Clash: Guaranteeing a fixed percentage of the principal capital independent of the venture's actual performance mimics an interest-bearing loan and breaks the PLS principle.

  • Islamic Alternatives: A Shariah-compliant "Halal Waterfall" resolves this by structuring the hurdle as a priority in profit distribution rather than a guaranteed yield. If the fund generates a 10% profit, the LPs receive the first 8%; but if the fund only generates 5%, the LPs only receive 5%, and the GP receives no carry. No clause can legally promise to make the investor whole if the underlying business fails to generate sufficient profits.

3. Interest-Based Leverage (LBOs) The "Leveraged Buyout" (LBO) is the engine of conventional private equity, historically relying on 60-70% interest-bearing debt to amplify equity returns and utilize tax shields.

  • The Shariah Clash: Taking on conventional bank loans to finance an acquisition is strictly haram. Additionally, Islamic PE funds must rigorously screen target companies; if a target's existing conventional interest-bearing debt exceeds roughly 30-33% of its total assets or market capitalization, the investment is prohibited unless the debt is restructured.

  • Islamic Alternatives: To achieve leverage without riba, Islamic funds must deploy asset-backed financing. This is often achieved through an Ijarah (sale-and-leaseback) structure, where a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) buys the target company's core physical assets and leases them back, matching the amortization profile of a conventional loan. Alternatively, Murabaha (cost-plus financing) can be used to fund the buyout via deferred payments. Crucially, in an Islamic LBO, the leverage must directly finance specific, tangible assets used by the company, rather than functioning as a general-purpose, free-cash-flow-based debt facility.

docs.title: 7.2 Structuring the Fund: GP/LP Dynamics
docs.text:
Shariah-compliant private equity (PE), venture capital (VC), and alternative investment funds fundamentally mirror the conventional General Partner (GP) and Limited Partner (LP) model but are engineered to replace interest-based mechanics with asset-backed, risk-sharing partnerships. To comply with Islamic jurisprudence (Fiqh al-Muamalat), these funds must strictly avoid riba (interest), gharar (excessive uncertainty), and maysir (speculation).

Fund Structuring: Mudaraba and Wakala Models Islamic funds are predominantly structured using one of two core contractual frameworks:

  • Mudaraba (Profit-Sharing Partnership): This structure serves as the most vivid Shariah equivalent of a standard GP/LP fund. The LPs act as the Rab al-Mal (capital providers), contributing 100% of the financial capital and bearing all financial risks. The GP acts as the Mudarib (investment manager), contributing labor, networking, and managerial expertise. Profits are shared according to a pre-agreed ratio. If the fund incurs losses, they are borne exclusively by the LPs (up to their invested capital), while the GP loses the value of their time and effort—provided the GP is not guilty of negligence, misconduct, or breach of contract.

  • Wakala (Investment Agency): In a Wakala structure, the LPs (Principals/Muwakkil) appoint the GP as their agent (Wakeel) to deploy and manage capital according to predefined investment parameters. Under this arrangement, the GP earns a predetermined agency fee (Ujrah) for their services. If the GP generates returns that exceed a specifically benchmarked "target profit," they are permitted to retain the excess amount as a performance incentive fee.

Fee Constraints and the "Halal Waterfall" Translating conventional fund economics—such as management fees, preferred returns (hurdles), and carried interest—requires careful structuring to avoid creating guaranteed fixed returns, which mimic prohibited riba.

  • Management Fees: Whether structured under Wakala or Mudaraba, management fees must be fixed or calculated as a percentage of assets under management (AUM), and never as a percentage of interest-bearing debt.

  • Preferred Returns (Hurdle Rates): A conventional 8% guaranteed hurdle rate is prohibited in Islam. Instead, a Shariah-compliant hurdle is structured as a "priority in profit distribution". For example, if a fund yields a 10% return, the LP receives the first 8%; however, if the fund only yields 5%, the LP receives exactly 5%. There is no structural guarantee or debt obligation forcing the GP to make the LP whole if profits are insufficient. Furthermore, under AAOIFI standards, the GP cannot be entirely cut out of any tier of profit; they must receive at least a nominal fraction (e.g., 5-10%) of the first tier of returns to preserve the validity of a true profit-sharing partnership.

  • Catch-up and Carried Interest (Carry): GP catch-up provisions and 20% carried interest splits are generally permissible. In a Mudaraba, carry is justified as the Mudarib’s agreed-upon share of the final partnership profit. In a Wakala, it is justified as a performance incentive granted to the agent for exceeding target expectations.

Governance under IFSB-6 Principles The Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB) governs the operational and ethical frameworks of Islamic Collective Investment Schemes (ICIS) through its IFSB-6 standard. This regulatory standard ensures that funds do not just cosmetically replicate conventional structures but maintain substantive Shariah compliance throughout their lifecycle.

  • Shariah Supervisory Board (SSB): IFSB-6 mandates the appointment of an independent SSB (or Shariah advisor) to provide ex-ante approval of the fund's methodology, review contractual relationships, and perform ongoing ex-post audits to ensure compliance.

  • Disclosure and Transparency: The standard requires rigorous disclosures regarding the methods of profit calculation, asset allocation, and the smoothing of returns (such as the use of Profit Equalization Reserves or Investment Risk Reserves) to protect the interests of LPs.

  • Purification of Income: Because PE and VC funds often invest in companies that may generate a small fraction of impermissible (haram) income—such as incidental interest from bank deposits—IFSB-6 and related guidelines strictly govern the "purification" process. Any tainted income must be calculated, isolated, and donated to independent charities to cleanse the investors' returns.

  • Conflicts of Interest: IFSB-6 establishes clear ethical boundaries for "ICIS Insiders" (the GPs/Sponsors), regulating how they manage internal controls, leverage, and the commingling of funds, ensuring the fiduciary duty to the Rab al-Mal is never compromised.

docs.title: 7.3 The 'Halal Waterfall' and Carry Mechanics
docs.text:
Private markets, including private equity (PE) and venture capital (VC), are a natural fit for Islamic finance because they emphasize profit-and-loss sharing, equity partnerships, and linkage to real economic activity. However, the conventional distribution waterfall—the contractual roadmap dictating how profits are shared between Limited Partners (LPs) and General Partners (GPs)—must be carefully adapted to comply with Shariah principles.

Here is how the core mechanics of the "halal waterfall" are structured:

Conventional 8% Hurdle vs. 'Priority in Profit Distribution' In conventional PE and VC funds, the European waterfall model typically entitles LPs to a full return of their contributed capital plus a preferred return (or hurdle rate), which is most commonly set at 8%, before the GP begins to collect carried interest.

Under Shariah law, a conventional preferred return can be problematic because it may resemble debt if it functions as a fixed, guaranteed return regardless of the company's performance. To ensure Shariah compliance, an 8% hurdle cannot be structured as a "guaranteed interest rate". Instead, it must be framed as a "priority in profit distribution".

  • If the fund realizes a 10% profit, the LP receives the first 8%.

  • If the fund only makes 5%, the LP receives only 5%.

  • Crucially, there is no contractual promise to pay the LP a fixed return if the business fails to generate sufficient profit.

Furthermore, AAOIFI Shariah standards allow partners to agree on varying percentages of profit allocation based on the magnitude of realized profit. However, this structure cannot entirely preclude any partner from participating in the profit. To satisfy this rule in a VC context, scholars often require that a small fraction of the first 8% (e.g., 5-10%) accrues to the fund manager, ensuring they are not completely cut out of the initial profit tier.

Catch-up Mechanics In a conventional waterfall, once the LPs achieve their preferred return, the flow of money shifts to a "catch-up" phase. This provision allocates distributions heavily to the GP until their share of the total profits matches the fund's overall carried interest percentage, correcting the temporary imbalance in profit-sharing created by the hurdle rate.

In Islamic structuring, catch-up provisions are permissible. Shariah scholars view the catch-up mechanism not as a guaranteed return, but as a legitimate, performance-based incentive designed to reward the manager for achieving targeted financial goals.

Carry under AAOIFI SS 46 as a Performance Incentive Carried interest (carry) is the performance-based incentive fee that GPs collect, typically 10–20% of the profits generated by a fund. To make this compatible with Islamic law, funds often utilize an investment agency structure, known as Wakala bi al-Istithmar.

In this structure, the GP acts as the agent (Wakeel) and the LPs are the principals. AAOIFI Shariah Standard No. 46 (Investment Agency) stipulates that a Wakeel is entitled to a predetermined fee, but may also be granted a performance incentive if the profits exceed a specified benchmark. This standard serves as a vital "translation tool" that allows conventional carried interest to be integrated into Shariah-friendly compensation. The carry is legally classified as a reward for the GP's labor, management skills, and performance, completely avoiding the characteristics of prohibited interest.

'Excuse' Provisions for Islamic Investors in Mixed Funds Many modern PE and VC funds are "mixed," meaning they raise capital from both conventional and Islamic investors. Because Islamic LPs are strictly bound by ethical screening rules, they cannot invest in companies involved in haram (impermissible) activities, such as alcohol, gambling, conventional banking, or excessive interest-bearing debt.

To solve this, mixed funds incorporate "excuse" or opt-out provisions into the Limited Partnership Agreement (LPA). These Shariah screening opt-out clauses allow Islamic investors to be excused from capital calls for specific portfolio companies that violate Islamic guidelines. This ensures that Shariah-compliant investors can participate in conventional platforms without their capital being exposed to impermissible investments.

docs.title: 7.4 The Leverage Challenge
docs.text:
The leverage challenge represents a primary "clash point" between conventional private equity (PE) and Islamic finance. While conventional leveraged buyouts (LBOs) typically rely on 60-70% (and sometimes over 75%) interest-bearing debt to maximize returns and create tax shields, Islamic finance strictly prohibits interest (riba). In an Islamic LBO, leverage cannot be general-purpose debt based on cash flow multiples; instead, it must directly finance specific tangible assets, limiting the debt strictly to the value of the assets being financed.

To operate within these boundaries, Islamic PE must address leverage at two distinct tiers:

1. Fund-Level Leverage At the fund level, Islamic PE funds are prohibited from using conventional interest-based subscription lines. Any leverage employed by the General Partner (GP) must be strictly Shariah-compliant. This is typically achieved by structuring fund-level leverage through Murabaha (cost-plus sale) or Musharaka (joint venture partnership) facilities.

2. Portfolio Company Level (The 33% Rule) When acquiring a target company, Islamic investors face strict constraints regarding the company's existing conventional debt. Shariah financial screening mandates that a target company's interest-bearing debt must remain below 33% (or 33.33%) of its total assets or a trailing average of its market capitalization, depending on the specific standard applied (e.g., AAOIFI, DJIM, FTSE, or MSCI).

This "one-third" threshold is derived from a Prophetic Hadith establishing that one-third of anything is considered "substantial" or "excessive," ensuring that the interest-based portion of a company's capital structure remains a clear minority. If a target company is highly leveraged, it falls into the prohibited zone. However, Shariah scholars generally allow a transition period—often up to three years—to restructure the company, pay down the conventional debt, and replace it with Shariah-compliant financing without disrupting the business's going concern.

Practical Responses and Structuring Alternatives To navigate these stringent leverage constraints and remain competitive, Islamic PE practitioners rely on several practical responses:

  • Growth Equity and All-Equity Deals: To avoid the legal and operational complexities of Islamic leverage and debt-to-equity swaps, many Shariah-compliant PE funds pivot their focus toward "growth capital" or "all-equity" deals. This strategy naturally aligns with the Islamic preference for genuine profit-and-loss sharing over debt creation.

  • Commodity Murabaha Facilities: When leverage is absolutely necessary for an acquisition, funds often utilize Commodity Murabaha (Tawarruq) or standard Murabaha facilities. These structures replicate the economic outcomes and liquidity of conventional debt by buying and selling commodities at a markup. A notable example is the 2007 buyout of Aston Martin, where 40% of the deal was successfully financed through a Murabaha instrument.

  • Ijara (Sale and Leaseback) Structures: Islamic LBOs heavily utilize asset-backed Ijara structures. In this scenario, a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) purchases a core asset (like real estate or machinery) from the target company and leases it back to them. The lease payments are specifically structured to match the amortization and payment profile of a conventional loan, creating the necessary leverage while maintaining Shariah compliance.

docs.title: 7.5 Private Credit and Acquisition Finance
docs.text:
Islamic private credit has emerged as a "huge white space" and a priority frontier in alternative investments, driven by massive institutional demand for non-correlated yields. While traditional private credit is fundamentally built on interest-bearing debt, the Islamic equivalent offers institutional investors "debt-like" returns (typically ranging from 8% to 12%) without violating the prohibition of riba (interest). The growth trajectory is substantial; a 2025 PwC and Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) report estimates that the combined private credit market in the GCC and Egypt could reach US$20 billion by 2030.

To operate within Shariah boundaries, conventional private credit mechanisms must be replaced by sale, lease, and agency structures—specifically Murabaha, Ijara, and Wakala—that deliver financing while maintaining enforceable security and creditor protections. These structures often take the form of Wakala (agency) and Murabaha (cost-plus sale) hybrids, which allow funds to deploy capital into mid-market businesses, real estate, and infrastructure while meeting both Islamic and ESG mandates.

For operational flexibility, specifically regarding drawdown-based financing and amortizing facility profiles, the industry heavily relies on Commodity Murabaha (also known as Tawarruq). The 2025 PwC/DIFC private credit market report acknowledges that Commodity Murabaha is the standard practice used to replicate the cash-generation and drawdown features of conventional private credit facilities. Through Tawarruq, a sequence of commodity purchases and spot sales is executed to provide the borrower with immediate cash liquidity, while simultaneously creating a deferred payment obligation to the financier.

However, the use of these highly engineered debt-replicating structures triggers a critical governance defensibility warning. Experts and regulators explicitly warn that the closer an Islamic private credit product comes to an interest-like certainty profile, the more the issuer must invest in Shariah governance defensibility and transparency. Because organized Tawarruq is frequently criticized by scholars for lacking genuine economic substance and mimicking conventional loans, its defensibility depends entirely on rigorous implementation.

To survive cross-border Shariah scrutiny, these structures must demonstrate genuine third-party commodity trading, a clean separation of contracts, and meticulously documented ownership and possession steps. Furthermore, when "Islamic wrappers" are utilized to channel funds into conventional private credit exposures, they must be rigorously stress-tested for permissible asset composition to ensure they are not merely cosmetic replications of conventional debt. Governance is not just a formality in this white space; it is the ultimate determinant of a product's bankability, legal enforceability, and reputational survival.

docs.title: 7.6 Infrastructure and Real Estate
docs.text:
Infrastructure and real estate are inherently compatible with Islamic finance because the core rules of Shariah mandate that all financial transactions be linked to tangible assets, actual economic activity, and clear risk-sharing, rather than the mere lending of money for interest. Because real estate and infrastructure generate highly visible asset ownership paths and predictable rental cash flows, they perfectly align with several foundational Islamic contracts.

Ijara and Diminishing Musharaka for Ownership and Rental To manage ownership and rental cash flows without violating the prohibition on interest, Islamic finance relies heavily on two primary structures:

  • Ijara (Leasing): Under an Ijara contract, the financier purchases and legally owns the asset, then leases its "usufruct" (the right to use it) to the client in exchange for specified rental payments. This model maps flawlessly to real estate and infrastructure because the investor's return is justified by the rent generated from the asset's use.

  • Diminishing Musharaka (Declining Balance Partnership): This is a co-ownership model highly favored in real estate and home financing. The financier and the client purchase the property jointly as partners. Over time, the client progressively buys out the financier's equity shares while simultaneously paying rent on the portion of the asset still owned by the financier. Ultimately, the financier's ownership declines to zero, and the client becomes the sole owner.

Istisna for Construction and Development For projects that do not yet exist, such as "greenfield" infrastructure, highways, or real estate developments, the Istisna contract is the primary financing tool.

  • Istisna is a forward-funding contract where a buyer commissions a manufacturer or contractor to build an asset to exact specifications for delivery at a future date.

  • Crucially, Istisna allows for staged payments tied to construction milestones, perfectly mirroring the drawdowns used in conventional project finance.

  • In major public-private partnerships (PPPs), Istisna is frequently paired with a forward Ijara; the Istisna covers the construction phase, and once the asset is built and delivered, the Ijara governs the operational leasing phase to generate returns.

Islamic REITs (Real Estate Investment Trusts) Islamic REITs allow investors to pool capital to passively participate in real estate equity, functioning much like conventional REITs but with strict Shariah boundaries.

  • Tenant Screening: The underlying properties cannot be leased to businesses engaged in prohibited (haram) activities, such as conventional interest-based banks, casinos, or venues predominantly selling alcohol or pork.

  • Income Thresholds and Purification: If a property has mixed-use tenants, the non-compliant rental income must be strictly limited (often capped at thresholds like 20% or 49%, depending on the jurisdiction and Shariah board). Any impure income generated must be isolated and "purified" by being donated to charity.

  • Leverage Constraints: Islamic REITs must use Shariah-compliant financing (like Murabaha or Ijara) rather than conventional debt, and they must carefully manage their debt-to-assets ratios to remain compliant.

Private Credit Funds Using Murabaha Conventional private credit relies on interest-bearing debt, making it a challenge to replicate in Islamic markets. However, the demand for high-yield, alternative investments has carved out a massive "white space" for Islamic private credit funds.

  • To replace conventional debt, these funds heavily utilize Murabaha (a cost-plus financing contract where the financier buys an asset and resells it to the client at a disclosed markup) or commodity Murabaha (Tawarruq).

  • This structure successfully replicates the amortizing, predictable cash flows of a conventional term loan while remaining legally structured as a trade transaction.

  • By utilizing Murabaha, these Islamic private credit funds are able to deliver "debt-like" returns of 8-12% to institutional investors, satisfying the demand for fixed-income equivalents without violating the prohibition on interest.

docs.title: 7.7 Restructurings and Special Situations
docs.text:
AAOIFI Shariah Standard No. 3 (Procrastinating Debtor): Default and Late Payments In Islamic finance, managing defaults and late payments is strictly governed by Shariah principles, primarily to prevent riba (interest). AAOIFI Standard No. 3 addresses the "procrastinating debtor"—a financially solvent borrower who delays payment without a genuine reason. The standard outlines specific parameters for handling such defaults:

  • Prohibition of Compensatory Late Fees: Unlike conventional loans that charge compounding interest on late payments, Islamic institutions cannot stipulate any financial compensation to be retained as income for a delayed payment, including compensation for opportunity loss or currency devaluation.

  • Charity Penalty Clauses: To maintain credit discipline and deter willful defaults, Shariah scholars permit the inclusion of a penalty clause. However, any late fees collected must be donated to charitable causes and cannot be recognized as bank revenue.

  • Acceleration of Debt: If a debtor defaults on a single installment, it is permissible to stipulate that all future outstanding installments become immediately due, ideally after providing a reasonable notice period.

  • Recovery of Actual Costs: While banks cannot profit from delays, the procrastinating debtor is strictly liable for any actual legal and administrative expenses the creditor incurs to recover the debt.

  • Right of Set-off: A bank may stipulate the right to recoup the defaulted amount directly from any of the customer’s other accounts (such as current or investment accounts) held with the institution, without requiring further consent from the debtor.

AAOIFI Shariah Standard No. 59 (Sale of Debt): Constraints on Distressed Strategies AAOIFI Standard 59 governs Bay' al-Dayn (the sale of debt) and fundamentally alters how distressed debt strategies can operate in Islamic markets. In conventional finance, distressed debt funds routinely purchase non-performing loans (NPLs) at a deep discount to face value.

  • Prohibition of Discounted Debt Trading: Standard 59 strictly prohibits selling a monetary debt for cash or for another monetary debt. Therefore, a conventional distressed strategy—buying a receivable at a discount—is invalid because trading money for money at a discount constitutes riba. Furthermore, discounting commercial papers or using factoring (buying invoices at a discount) is prohibited unless exchanged for a tangible commodity or ascertained usufruct.

  • Restructuring Constraints: When restructuring a distressed company, the creditor cannot roll over the debt into a new term with an increased mark-up or higher principal, as this mimics pre-Islamic riba (increasing debt for time). Restructurings must therefore rely on alternative mechanisms such as novation, debt-to-equity swaps, or the sale of underlying physical assets.

  • Secondary Market Tradability: For a hybrid Sukuk or investment portfolio containing debt (like Murabaha receivables) to be tradable, it must maintain a minimum "tangibility ratio" of physical assets or usufructs (typically at least 30% to 33%). If the tangible assets drop below this threshold, the instrument becomes non-negotiable and cannot be freely traded for cash.

Different Enforcement Paths: Murabaha vs. Ijara vs. Conventional Loans Because Islamic finance relies on trade and lease contracts rather than direct money-lending, the legal nature of the obligation drastically changes the enforcement path during a restructuring or default.

1. Conventional Loans

  • Nature: A direct debtor-creditor relationship based on the time value of money.

  • Enforcement: The bank is a secured creditor. Upon default, the bank accelerates the principal plus compounding default interest, sues for the monetary claim, and enforces its security interest against the borrower's collateral. The underlying asset's destruction does not absolve the borrower of the debt obligation.

2. Murabaha (Cost-Plus Sale)

  • Nature: A buyer-seller relationship where the bank purchases an asset and sells it to the customer on a deferred payment basis, creating a fixed debt.

  • Enforcement: Because Murabaha creates a debt obligation, the bank holds a claim for the unpaid deferred price. However, the profit margin is fixed and cannot increase due to default. If the client defaults and enters bankruptcy, Islamic law grants the seller (the bank) a priority right to repossess the specific asset if it remains in its original condition, bypassing the standard unsecured creditor queue. If the bank holds a mortgage over the asset, it can enforce the sale of the asset to recover the exact debt amount, returning any surplus to the customer.

3. Ijara (Leasing)

  • Nature: A lessor-lessee relationship. The bank retains legal ownership of the physical asset and leases the usufruct (right of use) to the customer for periodic rent.

  • Enforcement: Because the bank already owns the asset, it does not execute a traditional foreclosure on collateral. Instead, enforcement usually relies on a Purchase Undertaking (Wa'd). Upon an event of default, the bank exercises this binding unilateral promise, forcing the defaulting lessee to purchase the asset for an "Exercise Price" that equals the outstanding principal plus accrued, unpaid rent. This effectively accelerates the debt and provides the bank with a direct monetary claim.

  • Total Loss Risk: A critical divergence from conventional loans is the "Total Loss" scenario. In an Ijara, if the asset is completely destroyed or permanently loses its function, the lease is immediately terminated and the customer's obligation to pay rent ceases. The bank cannot demand continued payment from the customer and must instead rely on Takaful (Islamic insurance) proceeds to recover its capital.

docs.title: Executive Refresher
docs.text:
• Musharakah and Mudarabah Enable True Equity Partnership: Unlike conventional equity, Musharakah requires all partners to share profits and losses proportionally to their capital contributions, while Mudarabah separates capital (Rab al-Mal) from management (Mudarib) with loss falling solely on the capital provider. These structures enable genuine risk-sharing without fixed-return guarantees — making them the preferred vehicle for Islamic private equity but requiring more sophisticated due diligence on underlying performance.

  • Istisna Paired with Ijarah is the Standard Project Finance Toolkit: In infrastructure and real estate development, the Istisna contract finances the build phase via a back-to-back parallel Istisna engaging the actual contractor, and upon completion the asset is leased under Ijarah to generate rental income servicing the financing. This Istisna-to-Ijarah transition requires careful legal documentation to ensure continuous Shariah compliance and clear title transfer at each step.

  • Diminishing Musharakah Dominates Real Estate Finance: Commercial and residential real estate is predominantly financed through Musharakah Mutanaqisah, where the bank and client co-own the property and the client progressively buys out the bank's share while paying rent on the bank's remaining ownership. The periodic purchase tranches must be documented as separate sale agreements — not embedded in the original financing agreement — to avoid creating a disguised debt obligation.

  • Islamic Private Debt Alternatives to Conventional Bonds: In private credit, Murabaha and Wakala facilities can replicate the economics of conventional private loans, while Sukuk Al-Mudarabah provides the Islamic equivalent of a corporate bond with upside participation. The key difference is that these instruments require genuine underlying transactions, physical or documented commodity transfers, or identifiable investment portfolios — pure cash lending without asset linkage is not permissible.

  • ESG Alignment Creates Double-Screen Opportunity: Shariah screening (negative screen on haram sectors) and ESG screening (positive screen for impact) are increasingly combined in Islamic private markets, particularly for infrastructure, renewable energy, and social impact projects. Islamic private equity managers are building 'double-screen' frameworks that satisfy both the institution's Shariah board and the ESG requirements of sovereign wealth fund and development finance institution LPs.

A) Splitting rental income equally between the bank and the client regardless of current ownership share

C) Setting a fixed annual return for the bank and passing all rental upside to the client after a preferred return threshold

D) Distributing all rental income to the bank until its full capital is returned, then transferring ownership to the client

2. An Istisna contract in infrastructure finance is typically paired with a parallel Istisna because:

B) Regulators require two independent Shariah certifications for any construction financing above USD 50 million

C) The parallel Istisna converts the fixed-price contract into a variable cost-plus arrangement aligned with SOFR benchmarks

D) Two Istisna contracts are required by AAOIFI SS 11 to legally separate the design obligations from construction obligations

3. Islamic Venture Capital (IVC) structures differ from conventional VC primarily in that:

A) IVC can only invest in technology companies with fewer than 50 employees at the time of initial investment

B) IVC funds must distribute returns to investors within 3 years of deployment under applicable Shariah rules

C) IVC uses Musharakah or Mudarabah to align interests, cannot charge interest on convertible instruments, must avoid haram sectors, and must generate profit-sharing rather than debt-based returns

5. The Khazanah-style Exchangeable Sukuk structure is used in Islamic private markets to:

A) Monetise equity stakes in operating companies while maintaining Shariah compliance, providing investors with potential upside through future share delivery at a pre-agreed exchange ratio

B) Finance the construction of new factories through a commodity Murabaha linked to equity performance indices

C) Convert conventional private equity returns into Shariah-compliant income streams for Islamic investors

D) Satisfy Gulf sovereign wealth fund requirements for Shariah-certified private market allocations with capital guarantees
